title: Ready-to-Send Letters for Parents
description: Short, polite letters you can copy and send: second opinion on an evaluation, school records, IEP meeting, Medicaid and SSI denials, and more.
summary: Copy-and-send letters for evaluations, records, meetings, denials and the move to adulthood.
intro: Knowing your rights is one thing. Knowing what to write is another. Each letter below is short, polite and specific, and each one points to the rule behind it. Fill in the brackets, send it, and keep a copy.

sections.h2: A Second Opinion on the School's Evaluation
sections.html:
Use this when you disagree with an evaluation the school did.

Subject: Request for an independent educational evaluation for [child's name]

Dear [name],

Thank you for the evaluation completed on [date]. I disagree with it, and I am requesting an independent educational evaluation at public expense under 34 CFR 300.502.

Please send me, in writing, information about where an independent evaluation may be obtained and the criteria that apply. I would appreciate a reply by [date, about two weeks out].

Thank you,
[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: a parent who disagrees with the school's evaluation can ask for an independent one at public expense (34 CFR 300.502). See the school fine print.

Send this as soon as you have a meeting date.

Subject: Request for education records for [child's name]

Dear [name],

Under 34 CFR 300.613, I am asking to inspect and review all of [child's name]'s education records. Our IEP meeting is on [date], so I would appreciate access before then. I would also like copies of the evaluations, the current IEP, progress reports, and any behavior records.

Please let me know when and how I can see them. Thank you for your help.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: the school has to let you inspect your child's education records, before any IEP meeting and in no case more than 45 days after you ask (34 CFR 300.613). See the school fine print.

sections.h2: Who Is Coming to the IEP Meeting, and a Copy of the IEP
sections.html:
Use this when the meeting notice is thin, or after the meeting.

Subject: IEP meeting on [date] for [child's name]

Dear [name],

Thank you for the meeting invitation. Could you please send me the names and roles of everyone who will attend, and the purpose of the meeting? I would also like to confirm that [time] works for me. I plan to bring [name, role].

After the meeting, please send me a copy of the IEP. Thank you.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: the meeting notice has to say who will attend, the time has to work for you, and you are given a copy of the IEP at no cost (34 CFR 300.322). See the school fine print.

Short and easy. Send it any time you have not been given the notice.

Subject: Request for the Procedural Safeguards Notice

Dear [name],

Could you please send me a copy of the Procedural Safeguards Notice for [child's name]? Thank you.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: the school has to give you the notice at set times and any time you ask (34 CFR 300.504). See the school fine print.

sections.h2: Days Out of Class and What Happens Next
sections.html:
Use this after a child with an IEP has been sent home more than once.

Subject: Days out of class for [child's name]

Dear [name],

I would like to make sure we are both counting the same days. Could you send me, in writing, the dates [child's name] has been removed from class this school year, including early pick-ups?

If the total is over ten school days, please tell me what services will be provided, who will provide them, and when we can meet to review the behavior plan. Thank you for working with me on this.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: removals can add up to a change of placement, and services continue after the tenth day (34 CFR 300.530 and 300.536). See the behavior fine print.

sections.h2: The Plan for After School, Starting at 16
sections.html:
Send this before the first IEP meeting that comes after your child turns 16, or earlier.

Subject: Transition planning for [child's name]

Dear [name],

[Child's name] is [age], and I would like the next IEP meeting to cover postsecondary goals and transition services under 34 CFR 300.320. Please make sure [he/she/they] is invited. With my consent, please also invite [agency, for example vocational rehabilitation].

Could you send me the current transition assessments before the meeting? Thank you.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: the IEP has to include goals and services for life after school, and your child should be invited (34 CFR 300.320 and 300.321). See the Turning 18 and 26 fine print.

sections.h2: Early Intervention: Dates for the Evaluation and First Plan
sections.html:
Send this after you make the referral.

Subject: Referral for [child's name], made on [date]

Dear [name],

I referred [child's name] to Early Intervention on [date]. Under 34 CFR 303.310 the evaluation, assessments, and first plan meeting are due within 45 days. Could you tell me the dates that are scheduled, and let me know if you need anything from me?

Thank you for your help.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: the first evaluation, assessments and plan meeting are supposed to be done within 45 days of the referral (34 CFR 303.310). See the Early Intervention fine print.

sections.h2: Medicaid Said No: Ask for the Reasons
sections.html:
Send this right away. It also protects your time.

Subject: Request for the reasons for the decision on [case number]

Dear [name],

I received your notice dated [date] about [child's name]. Could you please send me a clear statement of the specific reasons for the decision and the specific regulations that support it? Please also tell me how to request a fair hearing.

Thank you,
[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: a denial notice has to include the specific reasons and the regulations behind the decision (42 CFR 431.210). See the Medicaid fine print.

Do not wait for the reasons letter if the deadline is close. Send this in writing and keep a copy.

Subject: Request for a fair hearing, [case number]

Dear [name],

I am requesting a fair hearing on the decision in your notice dated [date] about [child's name]. I would also like to know whether an expedited hearing is available. Please confirm receipt of this request in writing and send me the next steps.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: you have the right to a fair hearing, and the state can give you no more than 90 days from the date the notice was mailed to ask (42 CFR 431.221). Your state may allow less, so check the notice. See the Medicaid fine print.

sections.h2: SSI Said No: Ask for Reconsideration
sections.html:
Send this within 60 days of getting the notice. Keep the envelope and write down the date it arrived.

Subject: Request for reconsideration, [name and last four of Social Security number]

To Social Security,

I received a notice dated [date] about [child's name]'s SSI application, and I disagree with the decision. I am requesting reconsideration. Please confirm in writing that you received this request, and the date.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: you can ask Social Security for reconsideration in writing within 60 days after you receive the notice (20 CFR 416.1409). See the SSI fine print.

Send this at least several months before the birthday.

Subject: Dependent coverage for [adult child's name], member [ID]

Dear [name],

[Name] turns 26 on [date]. Could you tell me in writing whether this plan continues coverage for an adult child with a disability, what documents you need, and the deadline to send them? Please also tell me the last day of coverage under the normal rule.

Thank you for your help.

[your name]
[phone and email]

Why you can ask: a plan that offers dependent coverage has to offer it until 26, and the rule notes that other laws may require coverage for some children (45 CFR 147.120). See the Turning 18 and 26 fine print.

sections.h2: Before You Send Any of These
sections.html:
A few habits make every letter work better.

  • Send it by email or another way that leaves a date stamp, and keep a copy.
  • Fill in the blanks and cut anything that does not apply. Shorter is better.
  • Ask for the answer in writing, and put a date on your calendar to follow up.
  • Be kind. The person reading it is probably carrying a full load, and a clear, friendly note is easy to say yes to.

These are starting points, not legal advice. Your state may have its own forms and deadlines, and your state's parent center can look a letter over for free. If the answer is no, the disagree-in-writing guide shows the next steps.

checked: Each rule named in these letters was checked against the text of the federal regulation it cites (34 CFR 300.320, 300.321, 300.322, 300.502, 300.504, 300.530, 300.536, 300.613 and 303.310; 42 CFR 431.206, 431.210 and 431.221; 20 CFR 416.1409; 45 CFR 147.120) at ecfr.gov. These letters are starting points, not legal advice.
